title: The Life Is in the Blood
summary: God commands that every ox, lamb, or goat slaughtered in the camp be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting as an offering, so that Israel will stop sacrificing in the open fields to goat demons. Eating blood is forbidden to Israelites and foreigners alike, because the life of a creature is in its blood and God has given blood for atonement. Game killed in the hunt must have its blood poured out and covered, and anyone who eats an animal found dead must wash.
story: Leviticus 16 dealt with the cleansing of the sanctuary once a year. Chapter 17 turns to what happens every day when an Israelite kills an animal. It opens the second half of Leviticus, which scholars call the Holiness Code (chapters 17 to 26) after its repeated call for Israel to be holy as God is holy. The first half of the book centered on the priests' work at the sanctuary; this chapter speaks to "Aaron, his sons, and all the Israelites" (verse 2), and from here on the whole people is drawn into the work of holiness. The chapter is a bridge: it still concerns altars and blood, but it moves toward the everyday life of households, which chapters 18 to 20 will take up.
historical:
The chapter assumes the wilderness camp, with the tabernacle in the middle and everyone living close enough to bring an animal to its entrance. The name Holiness Code was coined by the German scholar August Klostermann in 1877, and most critical scholars treat chapters 17 to 26 as a distinct body of law. Some, including Jacob Milgrom and Israel Knohl, have argued that the Holiness material comes from a priestly school later than the one behind Leviticus 1 to 16, which edited and extended the earlier laws; others date it earlier; traditional readers see the whole book as a unity from Moses' time. What is clear on every view is that this chapter centralizes worship at one altar, a concern that returns in Deuteronomy 12 and in the later history of Israel's kings, who were judged by whether they removed the outlying shrines.

The "goat demons" of verse 7 point to a real practice. The same Hebrew word appears in Isaiah 13:21 and 34:14 for creatures that haunt ruins, and 2 Chronicles 11:15 says Jeroboam appointed priests for them. In the ancient Near East the desert and open country were widely thought to be home to spirits that had to be placated, and killing an animal in a field could easily become an offering to them.
cultural:
In Israel, as across the ancient world, meat was not an everyday food. Most families ate it on feast days or when guests came, and killing a domestic animal was often an act of worship as much as butchery. The law here turns every such killing into a peace offering (a shared meal in which part of the animal went to God, part to the priest, and the rest to the worshiper's household), eaten in God's presence. That both honored the animal's life and cut off the easy drift into offering it to other powers.

The ban on eating blood goes back to God's word to Noah in Genesis 9:4, given before there was an Israel, and this chapter extends it beyond Israel too: the resident foreigner is named five times. Jewish practice developed careful methods of slaughter and salting to drain blood from meat, and when the early church met in Jerusalem to decide what to ask of Gentile believers, abstaining "from blood" was one of the four requests (Acts 15:20, 29). A hunter's game, which could not be brought to the altar, was treated with the same respect: its blood was poured out and covered with dirt, returned to the ground rather than consumed.
literary: The chapter is law in five short paragraphs, most introduced by a formula such as "Anyone from the house of Israel" and each carrying a penalty. The first two paragraphs deal with where animals are killed and offered (verses 3 to 9), the next two with blood (verses 10 to 14), and the last with carcasses (verses 15 to 16). Several paragraphs give their reasons, and the reasons carry the chapter's theology. Verse 11 stands at the center, where God explains in the first person why blood matters: "I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar". The phrase about the life of the flesh being in the blood repeats three times in verses 11 and 14, driving the point home.

outline.t: A word for the priests and all Israel
Slaughter at the tent, not in the fields for goat demons
Every burnt offering and sacrifice brought to the tent
No eating blood: the life is in the blood
Game from the hunt: pour out the blood and cover it
Eating what died on its own

doctrines.note: Verse 11 is the Old Testament's clearest statement of why sacrifice involves blood: the blood carries the animal's life, and God himself has given it as the means of atonement. Atonement is God's gift, not a human technique for managing him.

The command to bring every animal to the tent is aimed at a specific idolatry, sacrifice to the goat demons of the open country. The text calls it prostitution, the Bible's recurring picture of worship given to someone other than the God to whom Israel belongs.
Holiness here reaches into ordinary life: how a family gets its meat, what a hunter does with his kill, what happens after eating a carcass. Nothing is too ordinary to be done before God.

words.note: Dam, blood. It occurs thirteen times in sixteen verses. Blood can mean guilt for killing (verse 4, where slaughter away from the altar counts as shedding blood) or the life that belongs to God and is given back to him on the altar (verse 11). The chapter keeps both senses in view: life is sacred, and taking it is never neutral.

Nephesh, here meaning life. The word ranges widely: throat, breath, appetite, living being, person, self. In verse 11 it appears in both halves of the sentence, the life of the flesh and atonement for your souls, which suggests a life given for a life. Interpreters differ on whether verse 11 speaks of ransom or of cleansing, but the link between the two lives is clear in the wording.

Sa'ir, literally a hairy one, the ordinary word for a male goat (it is used for the goats of chapter 16). Here it names goat-shaped spirits of the wild that people sacrificed to. Older translations rendered it satyrs, after the goat-legged creatures of Greek myth, though the Hebrew belongs to its own world of desert spirits.

Karat, to cut off. Being cut off from one's people is the penalty in verses 4, 9, 10, and 14. Its meaning is debated: execution by the community, a death at God's hand, the ending of a person's family line, or exclusion from the covenant people. In verse 10 God says he himself will do it, which suggests divine judgment rather than a court sentence.

christ: Leviticus 17:11 supplies the logic behind the New Testament's language about the blood of Christ. When Hebrews says that "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Hebrews 9:22), and Peter says believers were redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Peter 1:19), they are drawing on the idea stated here: blood is life given up, and God appoints it for atonement. Against this background, Jesus' words in John 6 were shocking to his hearers: "unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you" (John 6:53). Many disciples found it "a difficult teaching" (John 6:60). The law forbade drinking blood because the life belonged to God; Jesus offers his own life to be received. Christians differ on how that is present in the Lord's Supper, but they agree that Christ's given life is the source of theirs.

hard.q: Leviticus 17 requires every animal to be killed at the tabernacle, but Deuteronomy 12 lets Israelites slaughter meat at home. Do the laws contradict each other?
hard.a: Deuteronomy 12:15 and 12:21 do permit ordinary slaughter away from the sanctuary, as long as the blood is poured on the ground, while Leviticus 17:3-4 treats killing an ox, lamb, or goat anywhere but at the tent as bloodguilt. Readers explain the difference in several ways. Many traditional interpreters see Leviticus as a law for the wilderness camp, where everyone lived near the tabernacle, and Deuteronomy as Moses adjusting it for life in a large land where the sanctuary would be days away; Deuteronomy itself gives distance as the reason. Some Jewish interpreters read Leviticus 17 more narrowly, as concerned only with animals intended as sacrifices. Many critical scholars see the two laws as coming from different circles or periods, with the Deuteronomic law reflecting the centralizing reforms of the later monarchy and the Holiness law representing a different ideal. On any reading, both laws agree on two things: blood belongs to God, and sacrifice must not drift to other gods or other altars.

questions: The chapter makes a family's ordinary meal into an act of worship. What ordinary parts of your life would look different if you did them consciously before God?
Israel drifted into offering sacrifices to the spirits of the open field without, perhaps, meaning to. How does worship of something other than God creep into a life unnoticed?
The law treated animal life as sacred enough that even a hunter had to cover the blood. What does that suggest about how we should regard the lives we take and use?
